en: Strike this accursed warrior
From every side!
You came to fight and now stand idle—
Damn you, people of the Kazakhs,
Such conduct brings you shame.
Aim at the head above
His tightly belted waist and cut it off!
This lion, who trusts
In bloodthirsty Manas’s son,
Who enters battle when commanded
And drives every foe before him—
Cut off the head
Of this rabid warrior!
Once that warrior is gone from sight
And your greater purpose prospers,
Then trample the foolish son of Manas
Down beneath your feet
And scatter all his herds!
Raid every one of his horses;
Seize all his wealth!
Pour forth volleys of gunfire;
Avenge our forefather, hero Köksö,
In precisely this manner!
Let a thousand spears thrust together
And deliver his punishment into our hands.
Give this slave who boasts of strength
The punishment he deserves!
Do it heedless of blood;
Slaughter all his people without remainder!
Bring anguish upon his nation;
Let not a single soul remain.
My people, this is my command:
Let there be a massacre!”
So saying, Ümötöy
Roared and poured out his wrath.
Becoming foes worse than the Kalmyks,
He summoned the whole multitude:
“Overwhelm him!”
They closed in, weapons undivided;
Once Ümötöy gave the order,
They seemed determined to spare no life.
All together they surged forward.
The dense host of Kazakhs, in plain sight,
Thrust their spears at the noble warrior,
Showing no intention of sparing him.
Their fierce guns cracked,
And together they overwhelmed him.
Their black muskets boomed;
Firing jezails and drawing bows,
The Kazakhs closed in as one.
Then Külchoro—
A lion-warrior surpassing the world,
A hero unlike all other men—
Could not endure the humiliation,
Nor the mindless violence Ümötöy inflicted
When he had come as an envoy.
When faced with such grievous assault,
How could the warrior refrain from destroying them?
When faced with still greater violence,
How could Külchoro merely watch?
He roared in fury,
Raising the battle cry of “Manas!”
He struck his gray horse on the flank
And took his slender spear in hand.
He wheeled and wheeled among them;
Ten died wherever he wheeled.
Five or six died at his waist,
Crying, “Brother, we submit!”
Six or seven lay stretched out,
Dead where they had confronted him.
Every wise elder
And the whole Kazakh people
Recoiled in terror at the attacking warrior.
“We have come to witness
The dreadful havoc of the jezail;
We have come, every soul together,
To lose our lives and die!
This hero Ümötöy
Has proved to be no protection at all.
That dark-hearted infidel,
Claiming Köksö’s blood-price,
Has come to gather
The tribute of Sary-Arka,” they said.
“He has come to scatter all the people
And slaughter them,” they said.
“He means to gather subjects and build a nation
For himself,” they said.
“He means to find his chance
And bring the people to utter ruin,” they said.
The people cried out and an uproar arose,
Their clamor spreading the tale.
Many Kazakhs dismounted:
“Keep the common people in your thoughts;
Seize and slay the troublemaker!
Is our blood the blood of swine?
Spare those who remain!
He was the one who began the quarrel;
What have all the people done to you?
Ah, hero, we beg your mercy!
You were a lion of mighty presence;
We submit ourselves to you!”
So spoke the teeming host,
And the people broke into lamentation.
Külchoro wisely perceived
How the multitude stood before him;
Whether they spoke or not, could it be denied?
Seeing the dense crowd clamoring,
Külchoro accepted their plea.
Without touching the common people,
The startled lion-warrior
Rode farther on.
Clad all in blue steel,
He reached Khan Ümötöy.
“From atop the bay horse,
At the face of his right shoulder,
By the edge of his spine,
There lies the measured spot.
If I guide my thrust without driving it through,
That trailing-robed Kazakh slave
Will be hurled from the saddle.
I shall stab close beside
The maddened fool
And take him bound for judgment
Before my lord and sworn brother.
Without killing or destroying him,
Without bringing ruin on my own head,
I shall take him bound to the council.
I shall bring this incurable great quarrel
Before the public assembly;
I shall bring this deafening uproar
Before the council.
I shall bind to public renown
The honor for which a hero dies;
I shall bring this merciless great mischief
To trial for its wrongdoing.
If Semetey approves Ümötöy’s words,
Let him strike and hew me limb from limb;
Let me cease to live
And renounce my uncle Semetey.
Though Ümötöy has fought me,
He is still my blood cousin;
I shall bind my kinsman
And take him to my uncle.
I shall tell my uncle,
‘Your friend has become your enemy.’
If the people see Ümötöy
And suddenly take fright,
Or unexpectedly call him an outsider,
Why should I treat him as kin?
If we meet, I shall cut off his head!
If he will not obey at all,
I shall renounce my uncle the khan!”
So saying, Külchoro—
A broad-shouldered master of the spear,
A deft man surpassing the world,
Who never withdrew once battle began,
Who never turned from a foe he engaged,
A grasping leopard of a man,
A sage with the wisdom of a saint—
Wore trousers of yellow hide
And rode the handsome gray horse.
Though countless hosts came against him,
He charged without thinking he might die,
A lion-warrior born to command,
A surpassing sultan among heroes.
At the face of Ümötöy’s belt,
At the edge of his bulletproof coat,
At the eye of his great mail,
Against the coat itself,
The impassioned warrior overtook him.
With one blow of the spear,
He struck hero Ümötöy—
The man well fitted to demand blood-price,
The sturdy man with a treacherous belly—
Preparing to sweep him down.
Ümötöy, son of Khan Köksö,
Was destined to see a different misfortune:
Külchoro hooked him away as he passed.
Then Külchoro wheeled back,
Tall as a pole,
Swooping like a hawk.
He reached the unhorsed Ümötöy
Before an arrow could reach him.
Your lion-warrior turned back
And confronted Khan Ümötöy.
Your impassioned warrior overtook him;
Before one could say a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Without killing or destroying him,
With all his robes and garments intact,
He put the blue mail upon him,
Rolled and bundled him,
And made the fallen warrior
Whine like a howling dog.
Leaving him sprawled like a craggy mountain,
He stretched Khan Ümötöy out.
At that moment your lion-warrior
Captured him alive
And bound him to the bay horse.
Saying, “Here is your kinsman and cousin,”
He brought him alive and bound
Before the falcon-hearted lion.
He stretched Prince Ümötöy
Down from the bay horse,
And mighty Külchoro
Took him from the saddle.
Then the warrior went to his uncle
And spoke to him:
“My lord, time after time
You send me into the crimson fire.
Your mighty Külchoro
Has never died wherever you sent him,
But when I tried to turn away, your kinsman,
This Ümötöy, would not relent.
He reared up in wrath;
Though I pleaded, he ignored my words,
And treated me shamefully.
He tore my coat with spear thrusts
And showed me wonders enough.
He would not heed me when I spoke;
My blood boiled, my heart burned,
And your lone-wolf cousin Ümötöy
Drove me into a towering rage.
They loosed arrows like falling rain
And fired bullets to take my life;
They broke my composure,
Set my blood boiling,
And sorely tormented my soul.
He brandished his pinewood spear
And demanded the blood-price of Khan Köksö.
When I reined in my horse, he would not stop;
At last my spirit could bear no more.
The massed Kazakhs gathered
And tried to bind my hands;
They meant to take as spoil
The coat upon my back
And show my eyes
A marvel no man had ever seen.
Since I first became Külchoro,
Since I first mounted a horse as Külchoro,
Since I first donned white armor,
Sat proudly astride my steed,
And charged the foe with a shout,
Since my fine mustache grew long
And I enjoyed the prime of youth,
Since I first charged the foe crying aloud,
Never have I faced such dire violence.
Since this warrior became a warrior,
I have never suffered such humiliation.
I offered six thousand head, led by horses,
As tribute, but he refused;
He would not lower his spear.
He drained much of my strength,
Tormented my soul,
And made my head spin.
When I offered horses and camels, he would not listen;
